title: Palestrina
hook: the composer whose music showed Trent that many voices can serve the words

segments.voice: Yesterday, the slave trade and the Church, and Peter Claver on the dock: permissions, protests, and a pope's letter. Your line was condemned and still done. What history did you read? Today, at the end of a heavy week, something to listen to. Day eight hundred eighty-two.

A small choir stands in a stone chapel in Rome. One voice starts a line. A second comes in a moment later, singing the same tune a little higher. Then a third, a fourth, until the room is full of separate lines weaving over and under each other, and none of them is the melody, and all of them are. It sounds like one breath. Bishops at a church council had worried that music like this buried the words of the Mass. The composer at the center of the story people tell about it was a choirmaster from a hill town near Rome. The town was called Palestrina, and so was he.
screen: `ONE VOICE, THEN ANOTHER.` → `LINES WEAVING TOGETHER.` → `A CHOIRMASTER FROM PALESTRINA.`

segments.voice: Today's word is polyphony: many voices, each singing its own line at the same time. First, the worry. At the Council of Trent, bishops complained that some church music had become showy, mixed with worldly songs, with so many voices tangled together that nobody could hear the prayer. The council's decree barred music that was lascivious or impure from the Mass, and some bishops pressed for words that could be clearly understood. Second, the legend. A story grew up afterward: the council was ready to ban polyphony altogether, until Palestrina wrote a Mass so clear and so beautiful that it changed their minds. That Mass carries the name of a pope, Marcellus. Historians aren't sure the story happened that way. But the story stuck because the music fits it. Third, the music. In Palestrina's writing the voices take turns, so the words come through, then blend again. Nothing shouts. No single singer is the star. Fourth, the place it holds. The Second Vatican Council gave Gregorian chant pride of place in the Roman liturgy, and said that other kinds of sacred music, especially polyphony, are not excluded. Choirs from cathedrals to small parishes still sing Palestrina at Mass. Psalm one hundred fifty ends, in the Douay-Rheims: "Let every spirit praise the Lord. Alleluia." Every spirit, every voice, each on its own line, and one prayer underneath them all.
screen: `TRENT WORRIES ABOUT THE WORDS.` · `THE LEGEND OF THE MASS THAT SAVED IT.` · `VOICES TAKE TURNS SO WORDS COME THROUGH.` · `CHANT FIRST, POLYPHONY WELCOME.` · then, large: `LET EVERY SPIRIT PRAISE THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to Palestrina. If you can, put on a recording of his music now, quietly, maybe the Mass named for Pope Marcellus. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to follow every line. Choose one voice, high or low, and stay with it for a while. Then let go and hear them all together. If you pray, let the music carry your prayer. If you don't, simply listen. No recording? Sit with the sounds around you, and pick out one at a time. The bell holds the time.
Polyphony. Many voices, each singing its own line at once, woven so the words of the prayer still come through.

Your line: many voices, one word. This week: martyrs in Vietnam, hidden families in Japan, Mother Seton, John Carroll, the king of Kongo, a hard history, and Palestrina. Today, listen for one voice you usually talk over. Day eight hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Catholic cathedral and parish choirs sing Renaissance polyphony, including Palestrina's Masses and motets, at solemn Masses, alongside Gregorian chant.

fork.setup: you're a choirmaster in Rome. the bishops say church music has become a tangle and nobody can hear the words. what do you write?
options: louder, showier music, so people pay attention.
music where the voices take turns, so the words come through.
fork.reveal: Palestrina's music lets the voices take turns and blend again, so the words come through. that's why the legend about him stuck.

original.note: Latin: polyphony, the word Vatican II's constitution on the liturgy uses when it says this music is not excluded.
